entities.summary:
Collection of Chinese poetry, comprising works dating from the 11th to 7th centuries BC Created by various authors. Dating to c. 700 BCE.

The Classic of Poetry is one of China's four great classics and a cornerstone of Confucian literature. It was compiled during the Zhou Dynasty (1046–256 BCE) by scholars who gathered and edited the works of earlier poets, such as the legendary poet Wen Yao (c. 1200 BCE). The collection contains over 300 poems, many of which were written on ancient oracle bones or other artifacts.

The Classic of Poetry has had a profound impact on Chinese literature and culture, influencing generations of poets and thinkers. Its themes of love, nature, and morality continue to resonate with readers today. The poem 'Li Sao' (also known as the 'Ode to the River'), which laments the decline of the Han Dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE), is still widely studied and admired.

The Classic of Poetry has been translated into many languages and has inspired countless adaptations, including films, plays, and musical compositions. Its influence can be seen in Japanese literature, particularly in the works of Matsuo Bashō (1644–1694 CE).

Despite its ancient origins, the Classic of Poetry remains a vital part of Chinese cultural heritage, offering insights into the country's rich history, philosophy, and artistic traditions.

The most famous line from the Classic of Poetry is 'Spring cannot be controlled; / Autumn cannot be stopped.' (Chu Fu, 'Ode to Spring'), which captures the timeless essence of poetry.

In 2016, a team of Chinese researchers discovered that the earliest surviving copies of the Classic of Poetry date back to around 500 BCE.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Classic of Poetry (Chinese: 詩經, Shījīng, 'Book of Songs' or 'Book of Odes') is the oldest existing collection of Chinese poetry, comprising 305 poems dated to the Western Zhou and early Eastern Zhou dynasties (c. 1046–600 BCE), and one of the Five Classics of the Confucian literary canon. It encompasses a remarkable range of poetic forms and themes: folk songs (guofeng, 'airs of the states') from fifteen different regions describing everyday life, love, courtship, farming, and seasonal change; court hymns (ya) used in aristocratic ceremonies; and ritual hymns (song) used in ancestral worship. Confucius himself reportedly edited the Classic of Poetry and attached great importance to it — the Analects records him saying 'If a man has not studied the Odes, he will be at a loss to express himself' — and the canonical status the Confucian tradition gave the collection ensured that Chinese literary culture and the Chinese classical examination system took it as their foundational poetic text for over two millennia.

The Classic of Poetry's influence on Chinese literary tradition is comparable to Homer's on the Greek tradition and the Bible's on Western medieval literature — it established the forms, themes, and allusive tradition within which all subsequent Chinese poetry was written, and a sophisticated literary-critical tradition of interpreting the Odes developed over centuries. The Confucian hermeneutical tradition interpreted even the apparently simple love songs as allegorical expressions of political loyalty and moral relationships — the 'fishhawk' poem that opens the collection ('Guan guan goes the fishhawk, on the islet in the river; beautiful is this noble lady, a good mate for the lord') was read as an allegory of the king seeking virtuous ministers. This allegorical tradition shaped the entire Chinese classical literary culture and its approach to reading literary texts as expressions of moral and political truth.
